description: Proving Ground talks from BSides Las Vegas 2023.

talks.title: Building a Culture of Cybersecurity: A Case Study Approach to Enhancing Risk Management
talks.teaser: Shows how to build a risk-aware culture by engaging technical staff and non-technical HR and marketing teams.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the perception gap between security practitioners and non-technical staff. Through audience polls, the speaker rates risk in two departments, human resources and marketing. HR handles sensitive payroll and personal records, often through PDFs, resumes and SaaS systems on endpoints that may not be fully controlled. Marketing staff meet outside contacts, which can bring unsolicited emails, odd attachments and invitations to meet off campus.

The middle of the talk follows a single lunch meeting that escalates step by step. Security staff hear alarm bells at each stage, while the marketer sees routine networking. The speaker argues that labels like high, medium and low mean different things to different departments, so teams should agree on definitions tied to what the organization depends on to make money. Suggested mitigations include access controls, verifying contacts, using official communication channels, and inviting non-technical staff into the discussion, including naming cyber champions within departments.

The closing point is that culture should be inviting rather than punitive. A fear-driven "no police" approach may get short-term compliance but little lasting engagement. In the Q&A, the speaker repeated that risk definitions should be set per organization and that relationship management helps bridge the gap. The takeaway is that security teams should empower staff to ask questions and understand their daily work.

talks.title: The Birds, the Bees, and the CVEs
talks.teaser: Explains how novel vulnerabilities in control systems and medical devices are disclosed and assessed across critical sectors.
talks.summary:
Iain Deason, a vulnerability analyst at CISA, began with how coordinated disclosure works for products that critical infrastructure relies on. The stages run from discovery and vendor validation to a patch or mitigation and a public advisory. Timelines range from about 30 days to two years, and control systems patch slowly because some sit underwater or in orbit.

Five case studies followed. A real-time operating system flaw spread through products from large vendors to small projects, and tracing the supply chain took over a year. A GPS tracker advisory drew press coverage that overstated the risk. A ventilator advisory with a low score still raised patient safety concerns, which pulled in medical expertise. A middleware standard flaw needed a consortium fix and mattered because it was used in dams and the International Space Station.

For practitioners, the takeaway was preparation. Publish a vulnerability disclosure policy, consider becoming a CVE Numbering Authority, and keep separate playbooks for pre-disclosure reports, zero-days and exploited bugs. Consequence-based analysis helps teams make risk decisions when the data is messy.

talks.title: OH-SINT: Merging OSINT Into RE Workflows to Simplify Analysis
talks.teaser: Shows how open-source pivots like C2 search and vendor documentation speed up reverse engineering of infostealer malware.
talks.summary:
A SOC analyst escalated an alert that looked like ransomware but matched no known samples, and the sandboxes timed out on it. The malware had been delivered through a lookalike download site that bundled trojanized copies of popular applications. By the time the team dug in, the command-and-control server was offline, leaving only a domain, a file hash and a little network detail.

The speaker walked through how open-source research filled the gaps. A user agent and a URI from the sample led to a vendor report on a stealer advertised on Telegram, which gave the ports and paths to look for. Searching Shodan for matching login pages and HTML titles surfaced live servers, and pivoting through VirusTotal relations exposed fresher samples, including a developer build uploaded before a sale. The talk also covered developer documentation, which sometimes explains the sandbox and virtual machine checks a sample performs, so analysts can change their setup instead of fighting obfuscated code.

The main takeaway is to treat reverse engineering as a cycle rather than a straight pass through the code, with each outside finding feeding new searches. The speaker listed tools for this work, including dark web search engines, alternative scanning databases such as Censys, BinaryEdge and ZoomEye, URLScan, SecurityTrails for DNS and IP history, and DNSTwist for typosquatting domains. The core message was that developers often publish what analysts need, and checking those sources early can shorten time to value.

talks.title: Enemy at the Gate, and Beyond: Detecting and Stopping Account Takeover
talks.teaser: Shows how to detect account takeover across MFA bypass, impossible travel, Okta session hijacking and AWS key misuse.
talks.summary:
The talk treats account takeover as two stages: obtaining access, through stolen credentials, phishing or an insider handing over logins, and then using that access, where a successfully authenticated identity can still belong to an attacker. It follows one intrusion chain that moves from a compromised mailbox to a phished user, a hijacked identity-provider session and finally a persistent cloud access key.

For each step the speaker presents a detection approach. Impossible-travel alerts produced millions of notifications at one large customer, so the team cut the noise by discounting shared corporate IP ranges that many endpoints use, trusting addresses seen routinely, excluding service accounts and building baselines of normal travel routes. For MFA bypass, a legacy basic-authentication client identifier in sign-in logs gives a reliable signal, which is then checked against endpoint data, past login history and mailbox activity such as forwarding rules. Okta session hijacking is spotted by grouping events per session ID and flagging changes in IP address, operating system or browser, using edit distance to ignore minor browser version updates. Newly created AWS access keys used from unfamiliar addresses are compared against a time-series baseline of normal IP usage.

The takeaways are that MFA alone does not stop account takeover, that correlating identity, endpoint and cloud sources reduces noise and adds context, and that detection has to feed a clear response workflow. Teams should also consider blocking legacy authentication through conditional access policies.

talks.title: Shining a light into the security blackhole of IoT and OT
talks.teaser: Explains why active scanning of OT networks often causes outages and outlines principles for scanning them more safely.
talks.summary:
The speaker, Huxley Barbee, draws on consulting work with manufacturing, transportation and higher education clients to explain how operational technology differs from IT. OT environments prioritise availability above all else, many devices run old software that is rarely patched, and many do not require authentication. He traces the erosion of air-gapped networks to around 2005, when organisations began connecting OT systems to the internet for remote management.

He walks through the Purdue model as an ideal that few organisations actually follow, and notes that default credentials and public vulnerability listings can give an attacker a practical path to exposed controllers. Passive network monitoring, the usual defensive approach, struggles with peer-to-peer site traffic and produces inventories with gaps and weak fingerprinting. Active scanning, however, can crash or freeze fragile devices through non-standard packets, security probes and heavy traffic.

To address this, he proposes five principles for active scanning in OT: avoid unusual packets, be careful with vulnerability probes, tune both packet volume and how traffic is distributed, fingerprint incrementally with benign queries first, and start small before expanding. The planned section on IoT devices was skipped for time. A practitioner should take away the need to inventory OT assets carefully and test scanning against fragile systems before running it broadly.

talks.title: The Brazillian DeepWeb. How Brazilian fraud groups work on Telegram and WhatsApp
talks.teaser: Shows how Brazilian fraud groups operate on WhatsApp and Telegram, and how tracking links exposed their IP addresses and locations.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who leads cyber threat intelligence work at a Brazilian company, argues that scams in Brazil run mostly through WhatsApp, Telegram and similar apps rather than the deep web. These groups mix social engineering with fake messaging accounts, fake websites, deepfakes that defeat identity checks, account takeovers and bank accounts used for money laundering. Suspects often sit in other countries, and police with limited staff and tools struggle to trace them.

To study the groups, the research posed as buyers of fake money and sellers of stolen-looking databases, then shared links that logged each visitor's IP address, browser, operating system and user agent. Some pages also asked for location permission or a selfie, which revealed more detail. Most visitors showed no VPN or proxy. A small share used VPNs or cloud hosting, and a few VPN users still exposed their real location through the permission prompt. Comparing the same links across Latin American groups showed more VPN use. The talk also described how a phone number tied to a Brazilian bank account could be linked to a person's name and other details through leaked data.

The main takeaway for investigators is to check their own operational security, including DNS leaks and VPN leaks, because one slip can expose the investigator. The speaker also stressed that public and private sectors need to share information more closely, and that carrier data requests can take months to return results, by which time a suspect may have moved on.
